## What you'll learn

- The steps from sequenced RNA to a table of counts per gene.
- Why reads are mapped to **all genomes at once**.
- Which choices in these steps change your results.

## The workflow

For a defined community, the genomes are known, so this is close to ordinary RNA-seq of a single organism, with a few differences.

::: {.compact-diagram}
```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  R["RNA reads"] --> Q["Quality control<br/>rRNA removal"]
  Q --> A["Map to all genomes<br/>bowtie2"]
  A --> C["Count per gene<br/>featureCounts"]
  C --> T["Count table<br/>(Parts 2–4)"]
```
:::

### 1. Quality control and rRNA

Most RNA in a cell is ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Library preparation usually depletes it, but some always remains, and the amount varies between samples. Check the rRNA fraction of each sample (e.g. with [SortMeRNA](https://github.com/sortmerna/sortmerna)). Remove rRNA reads, or simply don't count them: count only protein-coding genes (CDS), as below.

### 2. Map to one combined reference

Concatenate the genomes of all community members into one reference, and map each sample's reads to it:

```{.bash .notest}
cat genomes/*.fna > community.fna
bowtie2-build --threads 4 community.fna community

bowtie2 -p 4 -x community -1 sample_R1.fastq.gz -2 sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  | samtools sort -@ 4 -o sample.bam
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Map competitively
Map to **all genomes together**, not to each genome separately. Related strains share similar sequences. Mapped separately, a read from a shared region would be counted once for every genome it matches, inflating the counts. Mapped together, each read goes to its best match, and a read that matches several genomes equally well is recognised as ambiguous instead of being counted for each of them.
:::

By default, bowtie2 reports one alignment per read. If a read matches several places equally well, it picks one at random, but gives the alignment a low mapping quality (MAPQ 0 or 1). We don't count these reads: in the next step we keep only reads that map uniquely, with a high mapping quality.

### 3. Count reads per gene

Combine the annotation of all genomes into one file, and count read pairs (inserts) per gene:

```{.bash .notest}
cat annotations/*.gff > community.gff

featureCounts -T 4 -p --countReadPairs -s 2 -Q 10 \
  -t CDS -g locus_tag \
  -a community.gff -o counts.tsv sample*.bam
```

- `-t CDS -g locus_tag`: count coding sequences, one row per locus tag.
- `-s 2`: the library is **stranded**, and reads come from the opposite strand of the gene ("reverse"), as with dUTP-based kits. Other kits give `-s 1` (forward) or unstranded libraries (`-s 0`). If you're not sure, run featureCounts on one sample with `-s 0`, `-s 1` and `-s 2`, and keep the setting with the most reads in the "Assigned" line of its summary. Strandedness matters in bacteria: genes overlap, and many are transcribed in antisense, so counting both strands mixes them up.
- `-p --countReadPairs`: count inserts, not individual reads.
- `-Q 10`: count only reads with mapping quality of at least 10. This removes reads that map equally well to several places (multi-mapping reads), so each counted read comes from one known gene.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Not every aligner and counter fit together
Be careful when combining aligners and counting tools: not all of them are fully compatible. For example, featureCounts can't recognise multi-mapping reads in alignment files made by BWA. Filtering on mapping quality, as above, takes care of this: BWA, like bowtie2, gives reads that map equally well to several places a mapping quality of 0, so `-Q 10` removes them.
:::

Other aligners and counters work for this step too. We have tested BWA with our own counter, salmon, and bowtie2 with featureCounts; in our hands all of them give very similar results. It's always best to test what works for your data.

## The result

A count table with one row per gene and one column per sample, plus an annotation table saying which genome each gene belongs to. That's where Part 2 starts.

## Check yourself

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("Two strains in your community share a 5-kb genomic island with identical sequence. You map each sample to each genome separately and add up the counts. What happens to reads from the island?", [
  {text: "They're counted twice, once for each strain", correct: true, why: "Each separate mapping finds them. Competitive mapping to the combined reference assigns each read once."},
  {text: "They're discarded as ambiguous", correct: false, why: "Separate mappings don't know about the other genome, so nothing is ambiguous to them."},
  {text: "They're split between the two strains", correct: false, why: "Not even with competitive mapping: there, these reads match both strains equally well, get a low mapping quality, and are removed by the quality filter."}
])
```

## Key points

- Map to **all genomes at once**, so each read is counted only once.
- Count **coding sequences**, with the right **strandedness**, and count inserts rather than reads.
- Count only **uniquely mapping reads**, by filtering on mapping quality.
- Check that your aligner and counter handle multi-mapping reads the way you think they do.
